name: Vitamin E oil / Bio-Oil

card.summary: Popular over-the-counter scar oils whose scar-fading claims are not supported by reviews of the evidence.
card.note: Vitamin E can cause contact dermatitis in some users.

quick.overview:
Vitamin E oil and cosmetic scar oils such as the brand Bio-Oil are marketed and widely used with the idea that they help scars heal or fade. Proponents of such products often point to the antioxidant properties of vitamin E.

Reviews cited by Wikipedia have repeatedly found insufficient evidence for those claims, and its Scar article says research shows vitamin E to be ineffective for scars.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant, and the proposed idea is that applying it to skin supports healing and limits scar tissue. Wikipedia reports reviews finding insufficient evidence to support this.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports vitamin E causes contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users and may worsen some scars, though another article notes allergy incidence is low despite widespread use. Products are sold over the counter.

lead: Vitamin E oil and Bio-Oil are over-the-counter skin oils that people rub onto scars, acne marks and stretch marks in the hope of making them smoother, flatter and less noticeable. Vitamin E is topical tocopherol, a fat-soluble antioxidant sold as pure oil, in puncturable capsules and as an ingredient in creams [1]. Bio-Oil is a branded cosmetic oil blend marketed for scars and stretch marks. For appearance, the appeal is a cheap, easy way to even out skin texture and tone on the face and body, including stretch marks that can appear with rapid muscle or weight gain.

Wikipedia's article on tocopherol notes that topical vitamin E is widely used for wound healing and scar reduction, and that reviews have repeatedly found insufficient evidence for those claims [1]. Its scar article reports that vitamin E has been found ineffective for scars, that it can cause contact dermatitis in up to a third of users and that it may make some scars look worse [2]. The tocopherol article, by contrast, describes allergic reactions to vitamin E derivatives as infrequent given how widely they are used [1].

In lifting and bodybuilding communities, Bio-Oil comes up as a product people try on stretch marks that appear during bulking phases or growth in the legs and arms [3][4][5]. Silicone gels and sheets are the better-studied non-prescription scar products, although a Cochrane analysis summarised on Wikipedia describes the supporting evidence as weak [2].

angle.text: People apply vitamin E oil or Bio-Oil to acne scars, surgical scars and stretch marks hoping to soften and fade them. Lifters also use Bio-Oil on stretch marks from muscle growth. Whatever their effect on the marks themselves, oils moisturise the skin surface.

paras: Topical vitamin E is sold as pure oil, in capsules that people puncture, and as an ingredient in creams and serums. Branded scar oils are typically blends of vegetable oils and vitamins, and Bio-Oil is the best-known example. The scar-oil category is distinct from silicone gels and sheets, which are the most studied non-prescription scar products [2].

Bio-Oil is a commercial scar and stretch-mark oil sold over the counter in many countries and widely marketed as a skincare staple. It is marketed for scars, stretch marks and uneven skin tone, and Patient.info describes its plant-based oils as providing hydration [8]. Pure vitamin E oil, by contrast, is a single ingredient that people buy separately, often in capsules, and apply on its own or mix into other oils [1].

Users apply the oils to healed scars from acne, surgery or injury, usually by massaging them in over weeks to months. The stated aim is a flatter, softer and less visible scar. Wikipedia notes that vitamin C and some of its esters, rather than vitamin E, are the topical agents it describes as fading the dark pigment of some scars [2].

Stretch marks form when skin is stretched quickly, as in pregnancy, weight gain or growth spurts, and are linked to rising cortisol levels; bodybuilding and hormone therapy are also listed as contexts [6]. Wikipedia reports a systematic review that found no evidence that topical creams and oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy, while tretinoin and hyaluronic acid are described as having reported benefit [6]. Bodybuilders on T Nation describe using Bio-Oil during bulking and for leg growth [3][4][5].

Vitamin E (tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant, and the rationale for topical use is that it might limit oxidative damage and inflammation during healing and keep the area moisturised [1]. Wikipedia reports that reviews have not found sufficient evidence that this changes scar outcomes [1][2].

Stretch marks, in the account quoted in consumer coverage, arise when sudden skin change ruptures collagen and elastin, and severity depends on genetics, skin stress, elasticity and cortisol levels [8][6]. Moisturising oils are applied with the aim of improving skin pliability and the look of the marks rather than rebuilding the dermis.

Reviews cited by Wikipedia have repeatedly concluded that there is insufficient evidence that topical vitamin E speeds wound healing or reduces scarring [1]. The scar article states that research has shown vitamin E and onion extract to be ineffective for scars [2]. Silicone gel sheeting has weak supporting evidence from a Cochrane meta-analysis, with the underlying studies described as poor quality [2].

Dermatologists quoted in consumer health coverage describe the evidence for stretch-mark products as limited. In a Patient.info piece, a consultant dermatologist recommends twice-daily application for about three months and earlier use for best results, and the page notes there is limited evidence that products prevent stretch marks and that not all creams and oils are clinically proven [8]. Users and manufacturers also point to moisturising: oils soften the skin surface and may make marks less conspicuous even where they do not change the underlying scar tissue.

Vitamin E can cause allergic contact dermatitis, with derivatives such as tocopheryl linoleate and tocopherol acetate implicated [1]. The scar article reports contact dermatitis in up to 33 percent of users and that it may worsen some scars [2], while the tocopherol article describes incidence as low relative to how often the vitamin is used [1]. A 2024 case report in an Indian dermatology journal described facial oil granuloma after almond oil and vitamin E oil were injected, which is a different route from topical use [7].
Patient.info advises checking ingredients if skin is very sensitive and avoiding use on broken skin or around active acne [8].

sections.h: Research on topicals for stretch marks
paras: The stretch-mark literature mostly concerns creams and oils as a group. The 2016 review above found proprietary creams with some preventive data and reported no effect for plant oils such as olive oil and cocoa butter [10]. The consumer health summaries of Bio-Oil's own studies rest on small trials listed by the manufacturer, which the summary says were not accompanied by methods detail [8]. Dermatologists quoted there describe stretch marks as harmless and common and note that treatment can make them less noticeable but they typically persist [8].

Studies of topical vitamin E for scars are summarised in reviews that report insufficient evidence for a benefit [1][2]. A systematic review of topical vitamin E in scar management (Tanaydin and colleagues, 2016) is reported by PubMed search listings to have found no significant improvement in scar appearance in three selected studies, with contact dermatitis among adverse events reported in two of six included studies [9].

A 1999 double-blinded, split-scar randomized trial in Dermatologic Surgery (Baumann and Spencer) enrolled 15 patients with closed skin-cancer excision wounds. Each scar was divided so one half received Aquaphor alone and the other Aquaphor with vitamin E, twice daily for four weeks, with assessment at weeks 1, 4 and 12. The authors reported no improvement from vitamin E, no effect or a worse appearance in 90 percent of scars, and contact dermatitis in 33 percent of patients [11].

A 1986 prospective randomized blinded study in the Journal of Burn Care & Rehabilitation (Jenkins and colleagues) covered 159 reconstructive operations for postburn contractures. Four months of topical steroid, topical vitamin E or a base cream were compared over a one-year follow-up. Neither active treatment reduced scarring, and adverse reactions were reported in 16.4 percent of patients on active treatment versus 5.9 percent on base cream [12].

For Bio-Oil itself, the consumer health site Patient.info summarises company-cited studies: a 20-woman study of abdominal stretch marks with twice-daily application for 12 weeks in which about half of participants showed improvement at eight weeks; a 38-woman study in which 95 percent noticed a "significant result" after two weeks; and a 2018 study of 80 people with scars and stretch marks in which 17 percent reported no benefit. The page does not state who funded the studies or describe their controls [8]. A systematic review of creams and oils for pregnancy stretch marks is described in Wikipedia's stretch marks article [6].

A 2016 systematic review in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (Ud-Din, McGeorge and Bayat) examined topical products for stretch marks across 11 studies. It reported level-2 evidence of preventive benefit for two proprietary creams (Trofolastin and Alphastria), mixed results for tretinoin, and no effect for cocoa butter and olive oil; the authors stated that no topical formulation had been shown to be most effective and called for randomized trials covering prevention and treatment [10].

Vitamin E and Bio-Oil are mentioned as inexpensive skin-care products for scars and stretch marks. On T Nation, one poster recommended Bio-Oil to another for stretch marks as a product aimed at scars and stretch marks [5], and others mention using it while bulking [3][4].

Within bodybuilding communities, stretch marks are discussed as a common by-product of rapid muscle or fat gain, particularly on shoulders, chest, thighs and arms. Lifters on T Nation mention Bio-Oil alongside other skin products when they describe bulking phases [3][4][5].

timeline.event: Randomized study of topical vitamin E and steroid after postburn contracture surgery reports no reduction in scarring [12].
Double-blinded split-scar trial of vitamin E ointment after skin-cancer surgery published in Dermatologic Surgery [11].
Systematic review of topical products for striae distensae published in JEADV [10].
A study of 80 people with scars and stretch marks, cited by consumer health coverage of Bio-Oil, is reported to find 17 percent with no benefit [8].
Case report describes facial oil granuloma after almond oil and vitamin E oil injection [7].

lore.intro: Bio-Oil appears in bodybuilding threads as a stretch-mark product people try during bulks and growth phases.

claims.claim: Bio-Oil helps stretch marks and scars
claims.believers: Posters on T Nation call it a product made for scars and stretch marks and say they use it during bulking [3][5].
claims.experts: A systematic review summarised on Wikipedia found no evidence that topical creams and oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy [6].

claims.believers: Users cite vitamin E's antioxidant reputation as a reason to apply it to scars.
claims.experts: Reviews cited on Wikipedia report insufficient evidence, and the scar article says vitamin E has been found ineffective and can cause contact dermatitis [1][2].

claims.claim: Applying oil early, before marks fully form, prevents stretch marks.
claims.believers: Users and some clinicians suggest using oils from the start of pregnancy or rapid growth and for several months [8].
claims.experts: Patient.info notes that there is limited evidence that products prevent stretch marks [8], and a systematic review described by Wikipedia found no evidence that topical creams and oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy [6].

claims.claim: Vitamin E ointment improves the look of surgical scars
claims.believers: Users and many consumer products cite vitamin E's antioxidant reputation for healing and scar appearance [1].
claims.experts: A 1999 randomized split-scar trial reported no improvement and contact dermatitis in a third of patients [11], and a 1986 randomized study found no reduction in scarring after burn-contracture surgery [12].

claims.claim: Plant oils applied during rapid growth can head off stretch marks
claims.believers: Lifters on T Nation describe using Bio-Oil through bulks and leg growth [4][5].
claims.experts: A 2016 systematic review reported no effect for cocoa butter and olive oil on striae, and some proprietary creams showed preventive data [10].
